scenarios.name: single, pension below the $10,000 per-person cap -- OK's retirement exclusion has no age requirement, so this and the next case vary income rather than age
scenarios.source: 2025 Oklahoma Resident Individual Income Tax Forms and Instructions (511-Pkt.pdf), Schedule 511-A instructions, printed page 17, line A6 'Other Retirement Income': 'Each individual may exclude their retirement benefits up to $10,000, but not to exceed the amount included in the Federal AGI.' Line A5 (Oklahoma Government or Federal Civil Service Retirement), same page, carries identical $10,000 wording. Neither line states an age requirement anywhere on that page; the only age reference on the page is the unrelated FERS Annuity Supplement note under line A3. OUT-OF-SCOPE FINDING, not pinned as a knownDefect in this batch: the same booklet's printed page 9 ('Standard Deduction' section) states the single standard deduction is $6,350, not the $13,550 in StateTaxData.swift's OK config, and printed page 38's 'Calculating Tax on Taxable Income of $100,000 or more' worksheet states tax at $100,000 is computed as '$4,562 plus 0.0475 over $100,000' for single/MFS, i.e. a 4.75% top marginal rate, not the config's 4.5% -- both are base-computation defects unrelated to retirement-exemption attribution and are left for whichever task owns Oklahoma's base bracket/deduction accuracy. This fixture computes against the CONFIGURED standard deduction and bracket table on both sides of the comparison so the only variable exercised is the retirement-exclusion attribution this batch targets. Using the configured $13,550 single standard deduction: 8,000 pension - 13,550 standard deduction is already negative, so Oklahoma taxable income is $0 before the retirement exclusion is even reached, and tax is $0.00 regardless of the cap or its attribution.

scenarios.name: single, pension above the $10,000 per-person cap -- no age gate applies so the cap is exercised the same way for a single filer whether the flag is set or not
scenarios.source: Same Schedule 511-A, line A6, printed page 17 (see prior case for the full quote). Pension $40,000 exceeds the $10,000 cap, so $10,000 is excluded regardless of attribution (a single filer never invokes the per-individual multiplier, so this case and the next single case cannot themselves expose the flag defect -- they establish that the cap and OK's bracket math behave identically for a single filer today, which is what makes case 3's MFJ divergence attributable to the flag alone). Standard deduction $13,550 single and the bracket table (0%/$0, 2.5%/$3,750, 3.5%/$4,900, 4.5%/$7,200) are both taken from the CONFIGURED StateTaxData.swift values, not independently re-verified against Oklahoma's own published $6,350 standard deduction / 4.75%-top-rate table -- see the OUT-OF-SCOPE FINDING in the prior case's source string for why, and why holding both constant here isolates the attribution variable this batch targets. Oklahoma taxable income = 40,000 - 13,550 - 10,000 = 16,450. tax = 0*3,750 + 0.025*(4,900-3,750) + 0.035*(7,200-4,900) + 0.045*(16,450-7,200) = 0 + 28.75 + 80.50 + 416.25 = 525.50.

scenarios.name: MFJ, BOTH spouses individually have qualifying pension income above OK's own $10,000-per-person cap -- the load-bearing case for this batch, isolating the missing exemptionAppliesPerIndividual flag
scenarios.source: Same Schedule 511-A instructions, printed page 17: 'Each individual may exclude their retirement benefits up to $10,000.' 68 O.S. Sec. 2358(A)(20) grants the exclusion to 'each individual', so a married couple filing jointly where each spouse separately receives qualifying retirement income is entitled to $10,000 per spouse, $20,000 total -- not to be confused with HB2190's proposed $40,000 figure, which remains in committee as of this fixture's writing and must not be treated as enacted; $10,000 per person is the current, CORRECT amount and Phase 5 must not 'fix' the amount itself, only its per-person attribution. Scenario: primary receives $30,000 from the Oklahoma Teachers' Retirement System, spouse separately receives $30,000 from a private-sector 401(k) rollover IRA, pooled pensionIncome = $60,000 (the fixture schema has no per-spouse income field; the split is narrative, matching how every other MFJ case in this batch establishes which spouse earned what). Correct exclusion = $10,000 (primary, capped) + $10,000 (spouse, capped) = $20,000. Standard deduction $27,100 married and the married bracket table (0%/$0, 2.5%/$7,500, 3.5%/$9,800, 4.5%/$14,400) are the CONFIGURED values (see case 1's out-of-scope finding on why these are held constant rather than independently re-verified here). Oklahoma taxable income = 60,000 - 27,100 - 20,000 = 12,900. tax = 0*7,500 + 0.025*(9,800-7,500) + 0.035*(12,900-9,800) = 57.50 + 108.50 = 166.00.

knownDefect.summary: exemptionAppliesPerIndividual is false, so StateTaxData.swift's OK config applies the $10,000 cap once household-wide instead of once per spouse, halving the correct $20,000 MFJ exclusion when both spouses independently qualify.

scenarios.name: MFJ, only ONE spouse has pension income -- the case that stops a naive doubling fix, because today's single-cap engine happens to land on the correct total here even though its reasoning is wrong
scenarios.source: Same Schedule 511-A, printed page 17. Scenario: primary receives $50,000 from a single employer pension; spouse has no pension or IRA income of her own this year. Correct law: only the primary's own income is eligible, capped at her individual $10,000; the spouse has no qualifying income of her own for any cap -- single or doubled -- to apply to, so the household total is still $10,000. This is deliberately IDENTICAL to what today's flag-off engine already computes (min(50,000, $10,000 single household cap) = $10,000), and that coincidence is the point of this case: a Phase 5 fix that sets exemptionAppliesPerIndividual = true without also verifying which spouse actually earned the pooled pension dollars would, for a couple in this exact shape (both spouses independently clear the age-59 fallback baked into TaxCalculationEngine.swift's ageQualifiesForExemption), double the cap to $20,000 and erroneously exempt income the non-earning spouse never had -- an OVER-crediting regression introduced by an incomplete fix, not a fix at all. Standard deduction $27,100 married (CONFIGURED value; see case 1's out-of-scope finding). Oklahoma taxable income = 50,000 - 27,100 - 10,000 = 12,900. Same married bracket math as the prior case: tax = 57.50 + 108.50 = 166.00.
